blocks.text: Networks and types of networks: LAN, MAN, WAN

A **computer network** is a set of computers and other devices (printers, phones, servers) connected by wired or wireless links so that they can exchange data and share resources such as files, printers and an Internet connection. Each device on a network is called a **node**. Networks save money (one printer serves many users), allow fast communication and make central backup possible.
A collection of interconnected autonomous computing devices (nodes) that can communicate and share resources using agreed rules called protocols.
Networks are classified by the area they cover:

blocks.caption: Types of networks by size
rows: PAN
Personal Area Network
A few metres around one person
Phone tethered to earphones by Bluetooth
Bluetooth, USB
LAN
Local Area Network
One room, building or campus
School computer lab, office network
Ethernet cable, Wi-Fi
MAN
Metropolitan Area Network
A whole city or large town
Cable TV network of a city, a bank connecting its city branches
Optical fibre, microwave
WAN
Wide Area Network
A country, continent or the whole world
The Internet, a bank linking branches in different states
Leased lines, satellite, undersea fibre

blocks.text: Size grows as PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN. A LAN is usually owned and run by one organisation and offers the highest speed and lowest cost per user; a WAN is built from many networks, often owned by telecom companies, and is slower and costlier.
The Internet is the largest WAN: it is a network of networks. Do not call a college campus network a WAN just because it has many buildings; if it stays within one campus it is a LAN.
Common mistake: students match "city-wide" with LAN. LAN = local (building/campus), MAN = city, WAN = country or world.
Network devices
Network devices join nodes together and decide where data should go. Each device works at a different level of intelligence.

blocks.caption: Network devices
rows: Modem (modulator-demodulator)
Converts digital data from a computer into analog signals for telephone or cable lines (modulation) and converts the incoming analog signal back to digital (demodulation)
Connects a computer or router to an Internet Service Provider (ISP)
Hub
Receives data on one port and sends a copy to all other ports
Does not look at addresses, so it is unintelligent; all devices share the bandwidth and traffic collisions are likely
Switch
Learns the hardware (MAC) address of each connected device and forwards data only to the port of the intended receiver
Intelligent, faster and more secure than a hub; used inside a LAN
Repeater
Receives a weak signal, regenerates it and retransmits it
Extends the distance a signal can travel because signals weaken (attenuate) over a long cable
Router
Connects different networks and forwards data packets towards the destination using IP addresses and routing tables, choosing a good path
Joins a LAN to the Internet; works at the network layer
Gateway
Joins networks that use different protocols and converts one protocol format to the other
Acts as the entry and exit point of a network; the most powerful and complex of these devices

blocks.text: A home Wi-Fi box often combines a modem (to talk to the ISP line), a router (to route data between the home LAN and the Internet) and a small switch (the Ethernet sockets behind it) in a single unit.

Hub versus switch: both have many ports, but a hub **broadcasts** to everyone while a switch sends **only to the destination**. Router versus switch: a switch works inside one network using MAC addresses, a router connects different networks using IP addresses.
Network topologies
A **topology** is the way nodes and links of a network are arranged. It can be physical (actual cabling) or logical (how data flows). The four required for CUET are star, bus, tree and mesh.

blocks.caption: Network topologies
rows: Star
Every node is connected to one central device (hub or switch)
Easy to add or remove nodes; failure of one cable or node affects only that node; easy fault finding
If the central device fails the whole network fails; needs more cable than a bus
Bus
All nodes tap into one common backbone cable, with terminators at both ends
Needs the least cable; cheap and simple for a small network
If the backbone breaks the network splits or fails; performance drops as nodes increase; hard to find faults
Tree
Hierarchy of star networks joined to a root (backbone) node; a mix of star and bus ideas
Scalable; good for large organisations with departments; branches can be managed separately
If the backbone or root fails, large parts are cut off; costly and complex to maintain
Mesh
Every node has a direct link to every other node (full mesh)
Very reliable because of many alternate paths; no single point of failure; no traffic jam on a link
Very expensive and hard to install because of the large number of links and ports

blocks.text: Number of links in a full mesh of $n$ nodes is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For 6 nodes this is $\frac{6\times5}{2}=15$ links, and each node needs $n-1=5$ ports.

blocks.problem: A computer lab wants to connect 8 computers in (a) a star using one switch and (b) a full mesh. Find the number of cable links needed in each case.
blocks.solution:
(a) In a star every computer is joined only to the switch, so the number of links equals the number of computers: 8 links.

(b) In a full mesh each pair of computers has its own link. Number of pairs = $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=\frac{8\times 7}{2}=28$.

Each computer also needs $n-1=7$ network ports in the mesh, against 1 port in the star.

blocks.text: Star failure rule: a failed **node** or its cable affects only that node, but a failed **central hub or switch** stops everything. Bus failure rule: a break in the **backbone** stops all nodes or splits the bus.
The Internet, URL, WWW and applications

The **Internet** is a worldwide network of interconnected networks that use the TCP/IP set of protocols. Every device has an **IP address**, and humans use names such as www.example.com which the **Domain Name System (DNS)** converts to IP addresses. The Internet is the infrastructure (cables, routers, servers); the **World Wide Web (WWW)** is a service that runs on top of it.

A system of interlinked hypertext documents (webpages) stored on web servers worldwide and accessed through the Internet using a browser and the HTTP or HTTPS protocol. It was proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN.
The complete address of a resource on the Web. Example: https://www.example.com/courses/index.html

blocks.caption: Parts of a URL
rows: Protocol (scheme)
https
Rules used to fetch the page; HTTPS is HTTP made secure with encryption
Domain name
www.example.com
Name of the web server, resolved by DNS into an IP address
Path
/courses/index.html
Folder and file on the server holding the page

blocks.text: **Applications of the Internet**

- **Web:** browsing, searching, online shopping, banking and learning through webpages.
- **Email (electronic mail):** sending messages and attachments to an address of the form name@domain. Outgoing mail is sent using SMTP; incoming mail is retrieved using POP3 or IMAP.
- **Chat (instant messaging):** real-time text, voice or video exchange between users, for example messaging apps and chat rooms.
- **VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol):** voice (and video) calls carried as digital data packets over the Internet instead of the traditional telephone line, so calls to anywhere are cheap or free.
Internet and Web are not the same: email, chat and VoIP use the Internet but are not webpages. Email addresses have @; URLs have a protocol and domain.

blocks.problem: Identify the protocol, domain name and path in the URL https://www.school.in/results/class12.html and say what DNS does with it.
blocks.solution:
Protocol is the text before ://, so it is https.

The domain name is the part after :// up to the next slash: www.school.in.

The path is the remainder starting from the slash: /results/class12.html.

Before the browser can contact the server, DNS converts www.school.in into the server IP address.
blocks.answer: Protocol: https; domain: www.school.in; path: /results/class12.html; DNS maps the domain name to an IP address.

blocks.text: Websites, web servers and hosting
A single hypertext document (usually an HTML file) that is displayed in a browser and has its own URL.
A collection of related webpages, images and other files stored under one domain name and linked together, beginning with a home page.
A website is made of webpages. A webpage is one document; a website is the whole collection, just as a book is made of pages.

blocks.caption: Static and dynamic webpages
rows: Content
Fixed; same for every visitor until the author edits the file
Generated when requested; can differ for each visitor, time or action
Built with
HTML, CSS (client side)
Server-side scripts and a database (for example PHP, Python, ASP) along with HTML, CSS and JavaScript
Speed and cost
Loads fast and is cheap to build
Slower and costlier to build and maintain
Updates
Author must edit the file manually
Content updates automatically from the database
Examples
A school notice page, a simple portfolio
Online shopping site, social networking feed, online result page

blocks.text: A computer (and the software running on it) that stores websites and answers browsers requests for webpages using HTTP or HTTPS. The browser is the **client** and the web server is the **server**.

A service that provides space on a web server so that a website stays online and reachable through the Internet all the time. Free hosting, shared hosting (many sites on one server) and dedicated hosting (a whole server for one site) are the common types.
To publish a website: (1) build the pages, (2) register a **domain name**, (3) buy or obtain hosting space, (4) upload the files to the web server, so that anyone can type the URL and fetch them.

Do not confuse a **web server** (machine or software that serves pages) with a **web browser** (client program that requests and displays them), and do not confuse **domain name** (address) with **hosting** (storage space).
Web browsers, add-ons, plug-ins and cookies
Application software used to request, retrieve and display webpages and other web content, for example Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Apple Safari and Opera.

**Browser settings** let a user customise the browser: choose the home page, default search engine, download location, text size, pop-up blocking, saved passwords and privacy options such as clearing history, cache and cookies, or private (incognito) browsing.

blocks.caption: Add-on, plug-in and cookie
rows: Add-on (extension)
Small program that adds a new feature to the browser itself or changes how it looks
An ad blocker, a grammar checker, a colour theme
Plug-in
Software that the browser needs to display or run a particular kind of content that it cannot handle on its own
A PDF viewer or a media player plug-in
Cookie
A small text file that a website stores on the user device through the browser to remember information such as login status, preferences or items in a shopping cart
A shopping site remembering your cart after you close the tab

blocks.text: Cookies are text files, not programs, and cannot run or spread like a virus; they can however track browsing, so privacy settings let users block or delete them. Add-ons extend the browser; plug-ins handle special content types.
A cookie is stored on the **client** (user) computer by the browser, not on the web server. Clearing cookies logs you out of most sites because the stored login information is deleted.

questions.stem: Which type of network is typically confined to a single school building or computer laboratory?
questions.explanation: A Local Area Network covers a small geographic area such as a room, a building or a campus and is usually owned by a single organisation. A MAN covers a city and a WAN covers countries or continents, while the Internet is a global network of networks.

optionRationale.1: A WAN spans countries or continents, much larger than one building.
optionRationale.3: A MAN covers a whole city or large town.
optionRationale.4: The Internet is the global network of networks and is not limited to one building.

questions.objective: Identify LAN by coverage area

questions.stem: The device that converts digital signals from a computer into analog signals for a telephone line and back again is called a
questions.explanation: Modem stands for modulator-demodulator. It modulates digital data into analog form for transmission over telephone or cable lines and demodulates incoming analog signals back to digital. The other devices do not perform this conversion.

optionRationale.1: A hub only broadcasts incoming data to all ports.
optionRationale.2: A repeater regenerates weak signals; it does not convert digital to analog.
optionRationale.3: A switch forwards frames to a particular port inside a LAN.

questions.objective: State the function of a modem

questions.stem: Which device regenerates a weakened signal so that it can travel a longer distance along a cable?
questions.explanation: Signals lose strength (attenuate) over distance. A repeater receives the weak signal, regenerates it to its original strength and retransmits it, thereby extending the reach of the network cable. This is why long cable runs in a LAN use repeaters, and why a repeater does not change the data or choose a path.

optionRationale.2: A gateway converts protocols between different networks.
optionRationale.3: A router forwards packets between networks using IP addresses.
optionRationale.4: A modem converts digital and analog signals.

questions.objective: State the function of a repeater

questions.stem: In the URL https://www.example.com/shop/cart.html, the part "www.example.com" is the
questions.explanation: In a URL the text before :// is the protocol (https), the text up to the next slash is the domain name (www.example.com), and the remainder (/shop/cart.html) is the path to the file on the server.

optionRationale.4: The file extension is only ".html" and is part of the path.

questions.objective: Identify the parts of a URL

questions.stem: Which topology connects every node to a single central hub or switch?
questions.explanation: In a star topology all nodes have a dedicated cable to one central device. A bus uses one shared backbone, a mesh links every pair of nodes, and a tree is a hierarchy of star networks.

optionRationale.1: A bus connects all nodes along one common backbone cable.
optionRationale.2: A mesh connects each node to every other node.
optionRationale.3: A tree is a hierarchy of connected stars with a root node.

questions.objective: Identify the star topology

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a switch from a hub?
options: A hub forwards data only to the intended device, whereas a switch broadcasts to all ports.
A switch forwards data only to the port of the intended device, whereas a hub sends it to all ports.
A switch connects networks that use different protocols, whereas a hub does not.
A hub uses IP addresses to choose a path, whereas a switch uses domain names.
questions.explanation: A hub is an unintelligent repeater of data and copies every incoming signal to all its other ports. A switch learns the MAC address of devices attached to each port and forwards a frame only to the destination port, giving better speed and security. Protocol conversion is a gateway function.

optionRationale.1: This reverses the roles of the two devices.
optionRationale.3: Joining networks with different protocols is done by a gateway, not a switch.
optionRationale.4: Neither uses domain names; a switch uses MAC addresses and routing by IP is done by routers.

questions.objective: Distinguish a switch from a hub

questions.stem: How many links are needed to connect 7 computers in a full mesh topology?
questions.explanation: In a full mesh every pair of nodes has one direct link, so the number of links is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For $n=7$ this is $\frac{7\times 6}{2}=21$. Each computer therefore needs 6 ports. So a mesh of only 7 computers already needs 21 cables, which shows why full mesh networks are costly.

optionRationale.1: 14 would be $2n$, which is not the mesh formula.
optionRationale.2: 42 counts each link twice ($7\times 6$) and forgets to divide by 2.
optionRationale.4: 49 is $7^2$, which would include links from a node to itself.

questions.objective: Count links in a mesh topology

questions.stem: In a star network, which failure causes the entire network to stop working?
options: Failure of the central switch or hub
questions.explanation: All data in a star topology passes through the central device, so a fault there isolates every node. A failed workstation or a cut cable only disconnects that one node, and adding a node is easy and does not disturb the rest.

optionRationale.2: A single workstation failing does not affect the others.
optionRationale.3: A broken cable cuts off only the node attached to it.
optionRationale.4: New nodes can be added by plugging into a free port.

questions.objective: Recognise the single point of failure in a star

questions.stem: Which device is used to connect a LAN to the Internet and to forward packets between different networks using IP addresses?
questions.explanation: A router connects two or more different networks and chooses a path for each data packet by looking at its destination IP address and its routing table. A hub and a repeater work only inside a single network, and a modem merely converts signal type.

optionRationale.2: A hub just broadcasts data and cannot route between networks.
optionRationale.4: A modem converts signals; it does not route packets on the basis of IP address.

questions.objective: Identify the router as the inter-network forwarding device

questions.stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes static and dynamic webpages?
options: Static: built using a database and server scripts; Dynamic: written only in HTML.
Static: requires a web server; Dynamic: does not require a web server.
Static: same content for every visitor; Dynamic: content can change with the visitor or database.
Static: content is always generated afresh for each user; Dynamic: content is fixed.
questions.explanation: A static webpage is a fixed file (HTML/CSS) shown identically to everyone until the author edits it. A dynamic webpage is built at request time, typically by server-side scripts and a database, so its content can differ by user, time or action. Both types are delivered by web servers.

optionRationale.2: Both kinds of pages are delivered by a web server.
optionRationale.4: This is the reverse of the real behaviour.

questions.objective: Compare static and dynamic webpages

questions.stem: A cookie is best described as
options: a program that automatically installs plug-ins
a small text file stored on the user computer by the browser for a website
a file stored only on the web server that hosts the website
questions.explanation: When you visit a site, the server asks the browser to save a small text file (cookie) that records login status, preferences or shopping-cart details. It is stored on the client computer, so the site can recognise you on your next visit. It is data, not a program.

optionRationale.1: A cookie is not a program and does not install anything.
optionRationale.3: Blocking advertisements is done by an add-on such as an ad blocker.
optionRationale.4: Cookies live on the user computer, not on the server.

questions.objective: Define a cookie

questions.stem: A college has 3 departments, each wired as a star network. The three hubs are joined to a main backbone switch. Which topology is this?
questions.explanation: A tree topology is a hierarchy in which several star networks are linked through a root or backbone device. Here each department star hangs from the main switch, giving a tree. A bus uses one shared cable; a mesh links every pair of nodes directly.

optionRationale.1: A bus has all nodes on a single cable, not hierarchical stars.
optionRationale.2: A full mesh has direct links between every pair of nodes.
optionRationale.3: A ring is not in the syllabus list and has nodes joined in a closed loop.

questions.objective: Recognise a tree topology from a description

questions.stem: Voice calls made over the Internet using digital packets are an example of
questions.explanation: VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) converts voice into digital packets that travel over the Internet, so calls can be made between computers or phones at low cost. SMTP and POP3 are email protocols and HTTP is used for webpages.

optionRationale.1: SMTP is the protocol for sending email.
optionRationale.2: POP3 is used to retrieve incoming email.
optionRationale.4: HTTP transfers webpages and is not used for voice calls.

questions.objective: Identify VoIP as the application for voice over IP

questions.stem: A bank has branch networks in Delhi, Mumbai and Chennai that run different protocols. Which device must be used at each branch edge so that they can exchange data despite the protocol difference?
questions.explanation: The key detail is that the networks use different protocols. A gateway translates between protocol formats and acts as the entry and exit of a network. A repeater only boosts signals, a hub only copies data to all ports, and a switch forwards frames inside networks that already speak the same protocol.

optionRationale.2: A repeater regenerates signals; it cannot translate protocols.
optionRationale.3: A hub broadcasts data and has no conversion ability.
optionRationale.4: A switch works within one network and does no protocol conversion.

questions.objective: Select a gateway for networks with different protocols

questions.stem: A network of n computers in a full mesh needs 45 links. How many ports does each computer need?
questions.explanation: Let $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=45$, so $n(n-1)=90$, giving $n=10$ (since $10\times 9=90$). Each node connects to every other node, so it needs $n-1=9$ ports. Total ports are $10\times 9=90=2\times 45$, which confirms it. This confirms that a 10-computer full mesh uses 45 links and 9 ports per computer.

optionRationale.1: 10 is the number of computers, not the ports per computer.
optionRationale.3: 45 is the total number of links, not ports per node.

questions.objective: Reverse the mesh formula to find ports per node

questions.stem:
Statements:
A. A hub sends incoming data to all ports, while a switch sends it only to the destination port.
B. A repeater is used to join two networks that use different protocols.
C. A router forwards packets between networks using IP addresses.
D. A modem converts between analog and digital signals.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is correct (hub broadcasts, switch is selective). C is correct since routers work with IP addresses. D is correct, which is the purpose of modulation and demodulation. B is wrong because joining networks with different protocols is the work of a gateway; a repeater just regenerates signals. So A, C and D are correct.

optionRationale.1: B is false, so this option containing B cannot be right.
optionRationale.3: B is false, and this option also leaves out the correct statement A.
optionRationale.4: B is false and this option omits the true statement D.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements about network devices

questions.stem: Which pair of terms correctly describes who stores and who requests a webpage?
options: Web browser stores and delivers pages; web server requests and displays them.
Web server stores and delivers pages; web browser requests and displays them.
Both web browser and web server only store pages; DNS displays them.
Web server requests and displays pages; hosting provider delivers them.
questions.explanation: In the client-server model the browser is the client: it sends an HTTP or HTTPS request for a URL and renders the response. The web server stores the website files (provided by a hosting service) and answers the requests. DNS only converts the domain name to an IP address.

optionRationale.3: DNS resolves names to IP addresses; it does not display pages.
optionRationale.4: Browsers, not servers, request and display pages.

questions.objective: Describe the client-server roles in browsing

questions.stem: After clearing browser cookies, a user finds that a shopping site has logged her out. The best explanation is that
options: the web server deleted her account
the modem lost its connection with the ISP
the plug-in required by the site stopped working
the stored login information kept on her computer was deleted
questions.explanation: Many sites keep a small cookie on the user computer to remember that a login session is active. When the cookies are deleted the site no longer finds that information, so it treats the visitor as new and asks to log in again. The account on the server and the network link are unaffected. In short, acknowledging the source is how a user avoids plagiarism.

optionRationale.1: Clearing cookies on the client does not delete accounts stored on the server.
optionRationale.2: A lost modem connection would stop all browsing, not just log her out.
optionRationale.3: Plug-ins handle special content types and do not remember login state.

questions.objective: Explain the effect of clearing cookies

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A router can connect a LAN to the Internet.
Reason (R): A router forwards data packets between different networks using IP addresses.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Connecting a LAN to the Internet means moving data between two separate networks. A router does exactly this by reading destination IP addresses and choosing the next hop, so the reason correctly explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: (R) is not merely related; it is exactly what lets a router connect a LAN to the Internet.
optionRationale.3: (R) is true, so the option claiming R is false is wrong.
optionRationale.4: (A) is true, so the option claiming A is false is wrong.

questions.objective: Relate the router function to Internet access

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A star network keeps working when one workstation fails.
Reason (R): In a star topology a single backbone cable carries data for all nodes.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: each workstation has its own cable to the central device, so one failed node does not affect the others. The reason is false because a single shared backbone cable describes a bus topology, not a star. Hence A is true and R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot be a correct explanation.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so option 2 (both true) is wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so option 4 (A false) is wrong.

questions.objective: Contrast star and bus topologies

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Every webpage on the Internet is a static webpage.
Reason (R): The content of a dynamic webpage can differ for different visitors.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: online shopping and result pages are dynamic and are generated when requested. The reason is true, since a dynamic page is built by server-side scripts using stored data and so can differ for each visitor, time or action. Hence A is false but R is true.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so no option that calls A true can be correct.
optionRationale.2: A is false, so option 2 fails as well.
optionRationale.3: A is false, so (A) true and (R) false is wrong.

questions.objective: Distinguish static and dynamic webpages in assertion form

questions.stem: Match the device or concept in List-I with its description in List-II.
questions.explanation: A modem (A) converts digital and analog signals (III). A hub (B) broadcasts to all ports (I). A gateway (C) joins networks with different protocols (IV). A repeater (D) regenerates a weak signal (II). So the code is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

optionRationale.4: This assigns the wrong descriptions to modem and gateway.

questions.objective: Match devices with their functions

right: I. Sends incoming data to all ports
III. Converts digital and analog signals
IV. Joins networks that use different protocols
